summary: A July 1975 survey of New-Protocol Telnet servers. It is a status snapshot that updates RFC 679.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the July 1975 progress check on which computers had built the new Telnet and which features they offered.

questions: what is the new telnet protocol
which hosts supported new telnet in 1975
subtitle: A July 1975 headcount of which ARPANET hosts had adopted the new Telnet protocol.

tldr.problem: The network was moving from the old Telnet protocol to a new one, and implementers needed to know which server hosts had made the switch.
tldr.mechanism: A surveying program, plus a few manual checks, probed each server host as seen by the New-Protocol User Telnet at BBNA, as of 10 July 1975, and the results were tabulated by socket and option.
tldr.outcome: Of 43 server hosts, 25 (58%) had New-Protocol implementations and 16 (37%) did not; two were of unknown status.

today: RFC 703 is a dated snapshot from July 1975 that updates RFC 679; the unit metadata lists its status as Unknown and shows no later RFC replacing it. Its numbers describe that moment only.

sections.title: What Changed Since the Last Survey
sections.content:
The report comes nearly five months after the previous one (RFC 679). Several new server sites joined and there was significant progress with the New-Protocol, and the author hopes the TIP implementation scheduled for the end of the year will encourage more.

SRI-ARC is no longer a server host. MIT-AI, MIT-ML, LONDON and OFFICE-1 added New-Protocol servers. LLL-RISOS, SDAC-44 and ARPA-DMS joined the network, and SCI-TENEX, Rutgers-10, USC-ISIC and SUMEX-AIM joined with New-Protocol servers. Host numbers in the text are octal.
sections.plainLanguage: Since the last check, some computers left the network, some joined, and several learned the new language.

sections.title: The Tally
sections.content:
Of 43 server hosts, 16 (37%) had no New-Protocol server, 2 (5%) were new hosts of unknown status, and 25 (58%) had a New-Protocol implementation. Within those 25, 13 (30%) ran the New-Protocol on sockets 1 and 27 while keeping the Old protocol on socket 1, 8 (19%) ran it on 1 and 27, and 4 (9%) on socket 1 only.

The hosts in the first group are the ones the author understands to be 100% correct under all protocols and conventions. Some servers listed as New-Protocol on socket 1 actually try to talk to both Old and New user Telnets, depending on the control sequences received.
sections.plainLanguage: More than half the computers had the new language. A few could speak both, depending on who called.

sections.title: The Per-Host Table and Options
sections.content:
A table lists each server host with its number, name, the state of socket 1 and socket 27 (Old, New, X for no server, or ? when it could not be reached), and the New-Protocol options implemented. Option codes: I# means option # is implemented incoming to the user (the server says "Will #"), and O# means outgoing (the server says "Do #"). The options tabulated are 0 Transmit-Binary, 1 Echo, 3 Suppress-Go-Ahead and 6 Timing-Mark.

Two hosts, RAND-ISD and ANL, could not be reached. Servers marked with an asterisk, such as SU-AI, return improper responses to some TELNET option requests. All data came from the surveying program plus a few manual checks.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is a report card: for each computer it shows whether it answers the old door, the new door, or neither, and which extra tricks it knows.

cells: New-Prot on 1 and 27, Old on socket 1
